title: Surdas's single line
hookLine: a single line: leave the company of those turned away from the Lord (Sarang, Surdas, ang 1253)

lines: ONE LINE, PINNED TO THE DOOR.
cards: Some parts of the Guru Granth Sahib run on for pages: long ballads, rows and rows of saloks. Then, in Raag Sarang, on the same Ang as yesterday's hymn, there's the name Surdas, and with it a single line.
No verses after it, no story around it. It sits there like a note pinned to a door on the way out. Somebody decided one line was worth keeping, and it carries Surdas's name.

teach.h: O MIND, LEAVE THE COMPANY OF THE TURNED-AWAY.
teach.b: Here is the line, in paraphrase: O mind, leave the company of those who have turned away from the Lord.

teach.h: BEMUKH: THE FACE TURNED THE OTHER WAY.
teach.b: The key word is bemukh: one whose face is turned the other way. Not a cartoon villain. Someone whose whole attention points away from God.
Who was this Surdas? Tradition tells more than one story about the name, and the Granth doesn't settle it. What it gives is the line, and where it puts it.
Just before it stands a hymn headed with Guru Arjan's mark and the name Surdas together, about the Lord's people who live close to the Lord.

So one page holds both sides of the same idea: the company that draws you near, and the company that turns you away. Now the hard part, because a line like this can be misused. It isn't a license to look down on anyone.

teach.h: SANGAT SHAPES A MIND, NOT A LICENSE TO JUDGE.
teach.b: Sikh teaching puts great weight on sangat, the company you keep, because company shapes a mind the way water shapes a stone, slowly and without asking.
The line talks to the mind, not to the neighbors. It doesn't say: judge them. It says: notice what you're sitting in.
People, voices, feeds and habits: some turn the face toward what matters, and some turn it away a little more each day, so slowly it's easy to miss. Surdas doesn't argue the case.
One line, and the choosing is left to you.

how: Sikhs speak of sangat, the company of those who remember God, as something that shapes a person, and gather in the gurdwara partly to keep that company; Surdas's line is read in that light.

o: with the face turned away from the Lord
one whose mouth speaks only harsh words
someone too ashamed to show their face

games.q: inside the line — tap the pairs.
p: the mind the line speaks to

s: Surdas's words in the Granth run to a long hymn
under his name the Granth keeps a single line.
the line tells the listener to judge others
it speaks to the mind about its own company, not to the neighbors.
a hymn about the Lord's people stands just before the line
it's headed with Guru Arjan's mark and the name Surdas together.

games.q: you notice one friendship keeps leaving you sour and turned away from what you care about. what does Surdas's line ask?
o: tell the friend everything that's wrong with them.
let the mind choose its company more carefully.
games.why: the line speaks to the mind: leave the company of the turned-away. it isn't a verdict on anyone, it's a choice about where you sit.

practice: Let the last few days pass in front of you: the people, the voices in your ears, the screens, the conversations. Without judging anyone, notice which left your face turned toward what you care about, and which turned it away.
If you pray, breathe out Waheguru and rest in the good company you found.

wordCard.voice: Bemukh. One whose face is turned away from the Lord: Surdas's single line, kept whole, telling the mind to leave that company.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: with the face turned away; the word at the heart of Surdas's line.

carryVoice: Your line: one line. Some teachings fit on a note pinned to a door. That's day seven hundred eighty-eight.
